common_name: Wonderleaf Pearl Millet (Leafy Hybrid Forage and Cover Crop Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is reliably warm; Wonderleaf is a leafy hybrid pearl millet bred for grazing and green-chop as well as summer soil cover.

directions: Broadcast or drill into warm, moist soil after the danger of frost has passed, since pearl millet germinates poorly in cold ground. Wonderleaf was bred as a leafier, more grazing-tolerant hybrid than grain-type pearl millets, regrowing vigorously after mowing or grazing while still building a dense summer canopy that shades out weeds and protects bare soil during the hottest part of the season. It is markedly more drought tolerant than sudangrass or corn and, unlike sorghum-sudangrass, carries no prussic acid risk, making it a safer choice where livestock may graze regrowth. Mow or graze before seed heads mature to keep the stand productive, and let frost terminate the planting at season's end.

common_name: Moxie Teff (Fast-Growing Forage and Cover Crop Teff Grass)

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine seed after the last frost into a firm, warm seedbed; Moxie is a forage teff cultivar bred for rapid regrowth after cutting or grazing.

directions: Mix the tiny seed with sand or dry fertilizer for even broadcasting, then roll or cultipack to press it into firm contact with a warm, moist seedbed, since Moxie germinates poorly if seed is buried deep. As a forage-type teff selection, Moxie establishes a fine, fibrous root mat quickly, tolerates both short-term drought and periodic wet soil better than most warm-season grasses, and regrows readily after mowing, making it useful for filling a short summer gap between cash crops with repeated cuttings of biomass. Terminate by mowing before seed set to prevent volunteers, or simply let an early fall frost kill the stand.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: Golden German Foxtail Millet (Fine-Stemmed Summer Cover Crop and Hay Millet)

planting.note: Sow into thoroughly warm soil after the last frost; Golden German is a fine-stemmed foxtail millet strain selected for quick hay curing and golden-brown seed heads.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed about 1/2 inch deep into warm, firm soil once summer heat has fully arrived. Golden German is a classic fine-stemmed foxtail millet strain, thinner-stemmed than coarser types like White Wonder, which lets cut forage cure into hay faster and gives it strong palatability for livestock. Its fibrous roots knit the topsoil together and its dense canopy suppresses weeds through the heat of summer, while the crop matures quickly enough to fit into short rotation windows. Mow before seed heads fully ripen to avoid volunteer plants the following year, then let an early frost finish off any regrowth.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: White Wonder Foxtail Millet (Tall Drought-Tolerant Summer Cover Crop and Hay Millet)

planting.note: Sow after soil is thoroughly warm; White Wonder is a taller, more drought-hardy foxtail millet strain than Golden German, grown mainly for hay and summer biomass.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into warm soil once the heat of summer has settled in. White Wonder grows taller and coarser-stemmed than Golden German foxtail millet and tolerates drought stress notably better, which makes it a dependable choice for filling a hot, dry summer fallow window when other cover crops struggle to establish. Its vigorous, upright growth quickly shades out competing weeds and produces substantial biomass for mowing and incorporation, though the coarser stem makes it somewhat less palatable than finer-stemmed millet types if grazed. Mow before seed set to prevent reseeding, then let frost terminate the stand.

common_name: Appin Turnip (Fast-Maturing Multi-Graze Forage Turnip Cover Crop)

planting.note: Sow in late summer, by roughly six weeks before the average first fall frost, for reliable winterkill and fast establishment.

directions: Broadcast or drill the fine seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since Appin establishes fast and can be ready for a first grazing or mowing in under two months. Bred as a multi-cut forage turnip, Appin produces a long, carrot-shaped root rather than a broad bulb, along with abundant regrowth after cutting, so it can be grazed or mowed more than once before winter. It reliably winterkills in colder zones when sown early enough, leaving decomposing roots and residue that add organic matter and open channels in the topsoil ahead of a spring planting. Where winters are mild enough that it survives, mow or graze before flowering to prevent it from setting seed.

common_name: Willamette Common Vetch (Pacific Northwest-Bred Winter Annual Vetch)

planting.note: Sow inoculated seed 4-8 weeks before first fall frost; Willamette is a common vetch cultivar developed in Oregon's Willamette Valley for winter cover cropping and grass-seed rotations.

directions: Inoculate seed with the correct Rhizobium strain before drilling or broadcasting it into a fall seedbed, then lightly cover, since Willamette establishes best with good seed-to-soil contact ahead of cool, wet weather. Developed in Oregon's Willamette Valley, this common vetch cultivar was selected for a lower proportion of hard, dormant seed than older vetch lines, giving it more uniform germination and reducing the volunteer-weed risk it can pose in following grass-seed or grain crops. It fixes a substantial amount of nitrogen over winter and spring, growing a sprawling, tendrilled vine that benefits from a cereal companion like rye or oats for physical support. Mow or terminate at early bloom, before pods begin to swell, to release nitrogen quickly and avoid reseeding.
